concepts.title: Java arrays and strings
concepts.overview: Java arrays use fixed-length indexed storage. Reading or writing a valid position is constant time; scanning or moving many elements is not. A String is immutable, so repeated concatenation creates additional objects; prefer StringBuilder when constructing mutable text.
concepts.mentalModel: Imagine numbered lockers: each index directly identifies a position. An array references a fixed collection while an ArrayList manages a growable internal array and occasional capacity expansion.
concepts.whenToUse: Use arrays when order, contiguous indexes, predictable iteration and low overhead matter. Use StringBuilder for many string edits and ArrayList when the number of items changes.
concepts.tradeoffs: Array insert or remove in the middle shifts elements in O(n). ArrayList append is amortized O(1), not guaranteed O(1) on each resize.
concepts.commonMistakes: Off-by-one bounds, mutating inputs inadvertently, and confusing an array's length with its largest valid index.
concepts.operations: Array index O(1); scan O(n); append to ArrayList amortized O(1)
concepts.realWorld: Arrays back search results and data batches; immutable strings represent request keys.

concepts.title: HashMap & HashSet
concepts.overview: HashMap maintains key-value associations, while HashSet only asks whether a key exists. Hashing converts a key into a bucket location, then handles collisions through equality checking and Java collection internals. Correct equals/hashCode behavior matters for custom keys.
concepts.mentalModel: Think of labeled lockers rather than rescanning a bag. A set records seen values; a map additionally records a count, index or other information about each value.
concepts.whenToUse: Reach for hash lookup when you need fast membership, deduplication, grouping, frequency counts or value-to-index relationships.
concepts.tradeoffs: Hash operations are expected O(1), but consume extra memory; order is not guaranteed by ordinary HashMap. TreeMap gives sorted keys at O(log n).
concepts.commonMistakes: Storing mutable objects as hash keys then changing equality fields, relying on iteration order, or checking the current item after inserting it when two distinct indices are required.
concepts.operations: Lookup/insert/delete expected O(1); worst-case assumptions depend on collision handling
concepts.realWorld: Indexes, caching, deduplication, feature flags, counting HTTP status codes.

concepts.title: Sorted arrays
concepts.overview: A sorted array supports comparisons that eliminate entire regions of the search space. Two pointers can merge sorted streams, find pairs from opposite ends, or partition an array in-place. Sorting first often trades O(n log n) setup for faster downstream queries.
concepts.mentalModel: Picture two readers scanning sorted lists without backtracking. Each pointer only advances, so their total work is bounded by the combined lengths.
concepts.whenToUse: Use when input is already sorted, when an in-place partition is needed, or when you can justify that one pointer move cannot discard a valid answer.
concepts.tradeoffs: Sorting an unsorted array may destroy original indices or order. Binary search requires sorted data and careful boundaries.
concepts.commonMistakes: Incrementing both pointers unnecessarily, forgetting equal elements, or sorting without checking whether original positions matter.
concepts.operations: Two-pointer scan O(n); sort O(n log n) typical
concepts.realWorld: Merging paginated feeds and reconciling sorted logs.

concepts.title: Prefix sum array
concepts.overview: A prefix-sum array stores cumulative totals so any interval sum can be obtained by subtracting two previously computed values. Sliding windows instead maintain a live contiguous segment as its boundaries move. The right choice depends on whether you need arbitrary range sums or a changing valid window.
concepts.mentalModel: Prefix[i] contains the sum of indices before i. Therefore sum(l..r) equals prefix[r+1]-prefix[l], with an extra zero at prefix[0].
concepts.whenToUse: Choose prefix sums for repeated immutable range queries, subarray-sum counting and negative-number arrays. Choose windows for monotonic conditions such as positive sums or distinct-character constraints.
concepts.tradeoffs: Prefix preprocessing O(n), then O(1) per range sum; dynamic updates require Fenwick or segment trees. A window often needs only O(1) or alphabet-sized auxiliary memory.
concepts.commonMistakes: Assuming a positive-sum sliding-window method still works with negative numbers; forgetting the initial zero prefix or using wrong inclusive/exclusive endpoints.
concepts.operations: Build O(n), range sum O(1); window scan O(n)
concepts.realWorld: Analytics rolling aggregates and moving time windows.

concepts.title: Sorted indexed sequence
concepts.overview: Random-access sorted sequences let you discard half of candidates with a single mid-point comparison. Binary search needs a monotonic decision rule, not merely a numeric-looking input. For answer-space search, you binary-search the smallest feasible result rather than an array position.
concepts.mentalModel: Maintain a range known to contain the answer, such as [lo,hi). Every comparison must strictly shrink that range, and termination must leave one possible boundary.
concepts.whenToUse: Use for search, lower/upper bounds, rotated arrays and minimal feasible capacity/speed thresholds.
concepts.tradeoffs: Requires O(log n) comparisons but assumes O(1) indexing; binary search on a linked list loses its advantage.
concepts.commonMistakes: Infinite loops from unchanged bounds, overflow in midpoint calculation, and wrong behavior on duplicates or not-found values.
concepts.operations: Binary search O(log n); binary search on answer O(log range × check cost)
concepts.realWorld: Database index seek; threshold tuning; capacity planning.

concepts.title: Singly linked list
concepts.overview: A singly linked list stores values in nodes connected through next references, allowing local pointer edits without shifting an array. Unlike arrays, finding the kth node requires walking from the head; random access is O(n). Dummy nodes simplify head insertion/removal.
concepts.mentalModel: Each node is a train carriage holding a reference to the next. Reversing a list reroutes arrows one at a time while retaining the original next node in a temporary variable.
concepts.whenToUse: Use for frequent constant-time insertion/deletion when the target node is already known, and for LRU designs with both next and previous links.
concepts.tradeoffs: No efficient random access; extra pointer memory; allocations hurt locality compared with arrays.
concepts.commonMistakes: Losing the remaining list before redirecting next, accidentally creating a cycle, and not handling null or single-node lists.
concepts.operations: Index O(n), insert at known node O(1), scan O(n)
concepts.realWorld: Chained queues and adjacency lists; pointer-heavy LRU designs.

concepts.title: Stack / queue (ArrayDeque)
concepts.overview: A stack removes the most recently added item (LIFO); a queue removes the earliest item (FIFO). Java ArrayDeque supports both efficiently, and is generally preferable to legacy Stack. Monotonic stacks/deques store only potentially useful candidates, enabling linear-time scans.
concepts.mentalModel: Stack = plates; queue = people waiting in line. When a deque holds indices in monotonic order, obsolete and dominated entries are discarded before they are needed.
concepts.whenToUse: Use stacks for nesting, undo, DFS, and next-greater relations; queues for BFS, scheduling and breadth-by-breadth processing.
concepts.tradeoffs: Deque operations at either end are amortized constant time; monotonic structures use O(n) worst-case memory.
concepts.commonMistakes: Calling ArrayDeque methods on null elements, forgetting to drop expired indices, and confusing stack order with queue order.
concepts.realWorld: Parser nesting, undo, task queues, streaming window maxima.

concepts.title: Call stack
concepts.overview: Recursion models problems as smaller calls whose return values combine into a complete answer. Every recursive function needs a base case and progress toward it. Backtracking explores alternatives but also undoes temporary changes when returning to an earlier decision point.
concepts.mentalModel: Visualize a decision tree: each edge makes one choice. The call stack stores where to return; the active path represents the partial solution under construction.
concepts.whenToUse: Use for combinatorial generation, tree DFS, partitioning and exploring constraints with early pruning.
concepts.tradeoffs: Recursive depth may overflow the Java call stack; branching searches are exponential unless pruning/memoization removes repeated states.
concepts.commonMistakes: Forgetting to restore mutable state, passing the same mutable list into all results, or missing a termination condition.
concepts.operations: For subset enumeration O(2^n) outputs; recursion depth O(n)
concepts.realWorld: Configuration search, parsers, directory walks.

concepts.title: Binary tree
concepts.overview: A binary tree node has left and right child links. DFS recursively computes properties of subtrees, while BFS processes nodes by depth. BSTs add an ordering invariant, but an arbitrary binary tree does not have sorted nodes.
concepts.mentalModel: A tree is a hierarchy with no cycles. At a node, either combine answers from children or place children in a queue for the next breadth level.
concepts.whenToUse: Use for hierarchies, expression parsing, recursive decomposition, file-system structure and range indexes.
concepts.tradeoffs: Balanced binary trees have O(log n) height; arbitrary skewed trees can have O(n) height and recursion depth.
concepts.commonMistakes: Confusing node count with edge count, assuming every tree is a BST, and ignoring empty subtrees.
concepts.operations: Visit all nodes O(n); recursion O(h) stack; BFS O(w) queue
concepts.realWorld: DOM trees, ASTs, org charts, indexes.

concepts.title: Binary search tree / binary heap
concepts.overview: A BST orders keys: left subtree lower, right subtree higher (with an explicit duplicate policy). A binary heap is a complete tree represented in an array where the parent is <= children (min-heap) or >= children (max-heap). Heap operations do not return a globally sorted traversal.
concepts.mentalModel: BST helps locate keys by comparison. Heap keeps only the current best priority at the root, with child index 2i+1 and 2i+2 in its array storage.
concepts.whenToUse: Use heaps for top-k, priority scheduling, Dijkstra frontier nodes and streaming medians; BSTs for ordered queries and rank traversal.
concepts.tradeoffs: Heap peek O(1), add/remove O(log n); ordinary unbalanced BST may degrade to O(n).
concepts.commonMistakes: Mistaking a heap for a sorted array, treating PriorityQueue iterator order as sorted, and using subtraction in comparators where overflow is possible.
concepts.operations: Balanced BST O(log n); skewed BST O(n); heap add/poll O(log n), peek O(1)
concepts.realWorld: Schedulers, recommendation feeds, finding top response times.

concepts.title: Trie (prefix tree)
concepts.overview: A trie stores string prefixes as shared paths through character-indexed edges. Each path represents a prefix, and terminal flags indicate which prefixes are complete words. Compared with hashing every full word, tries offer direct prefix navigation and shared storage for common initial characters.
concepts.mentalModel: Imagine a dictionary organized by the next letter at each step: c→a→t. The node for cat is terminal; the node for ca may or may not be a complete word.
concepts.whenToUse: Useful for autocomplete, spell-check, dictionary prefix search, routing prefixes and multiword grid search.
concepts.tradeoffs: Lookup depends on string length, O(L), not number of entries. Nodes can be memory-heavy with 26-element arrays for sparse branches.
concepts.commonMistakes: Forgetting terminal flags, assuming input is lowercase ASCII when it is not, and failing to prune cyclic board paths.
concepts.operations: Insert/search O(word length), memory O(total stored characters)
concepts.realWorld: Autocomplete, routing prefixes, spell check.

concepts.title: Interval list
concepts.overview: Intervals express bookings, reservations, ranges and lifetimes using a start and end. Before solving, decide whether endpoints are inclusive or half-open. Sorting intervals reveals merge order and allows greedy choices based on start or earliest finishing time.
concepts.mentalModel: Picture time blocks along a ruler. Overlapping blocks form a continuous merged block; if maximizing non-overlapping choices, shorter finishing time leaves more room.
concepts.whenToUse: Use for calendars, execution scheduling, rate-limit windows, meeting rooms and resource reservations.
concepts.tradeoffs: Most interval algorithms are O(n log n) due to sorting, with linear scans afterward.
concepts.commonMistakes: Using <= rather than < for half-open overlap, sorting by start when a proof requires end time, or forgetting to merge repeated overlaps.
concepts.operations: Sort O(n log n), sweep O(n)
concepts.realWorld: Booking windows, CPU scheduling, calendar availability.

concepts.title: Adjacency list
concepts.overview: A graph has vertices and edges, directed or undirected. An adjacency list stores each vertex's neighbors in space proportional to V+E, unlike a dense adjacency matrix. BFS expands equally far vertices by layers, while DFS follows a path before returning.
concepts.mentalModel: A grid with four-direction movement is an implicit graph. Visiting every reachable cell marks one connected component; repeating from an unvisited cell discovers another island.
concepts.whenToUse: Use for reachability, dependencies, network services, connected components, mazes and shortest unweighted routes.
concepts.tradeoffs: BFS and DFS each visit V vertices and E edges at most a constant number of times, O(V+E).
concepts.commonMistakes: Not marking visited before enqueueing BFS neighbors, mixing directed and undirected edges, or using recursion on extremely deep graphs without considering stack size.
concepts.operations: BFS/DFS O(V+E), space O(V) for visited/frontier
concepts.realWorld: Service dependencies, maps, social networks, workflow DAGs.

concepts.codeLabel: Applied Java example: Count Islands in a Binary Grid
concepts.timeComplexity: BFS/DFS O(V+E), space O(V) for visited/frontier
steps: Scan each grid cell row by row. Skip water cells.
When an unvisited land cell is found, increment the island count, mark that cell as water, and enqueue its coordinates.
Process the queue: for each cell, inspect its four neighbors. For every in-bounds land neighbor, mark it as water immediately and enqueue it.
When the queue empties, the whole connected island has been visited. Continue scanning for other land cells.
Return the island count. Marking before enqueueing avoids adding the same cell repeatedly.

concepts.title: Disjoint-set union (Union-Find)
concepts.overview: Union-Find, also called disjoint-set union (DSU), tracks which nodes are already connected. Each set has a representative root; union combines sets, and find locates a root. Path compression and union-by-rank keep operations near constant amortized time.
concepts.mentalModel: Imagine groups of people wearing a shared badge. Two nodes with identical leaders already belong to one connected component; union merges two groups by connecting their leaders.
concepts.whenToUse: Use for cycle detection in undirected graphs, connectivity queries, Kruskal MST and clustering.
concepts.tradeoffs: Amortized O(α(n)) per find/union; DSU does not support deleting edges efficiently or give shortest paths.
concepts.commonMistakes: Skipping path compression/size balancing, confusing directed cycles with undirected DSU use, or failing to count initially isolated nodes.
concepts.operations: Union/find amortized O(α(n)); topo sort O(V+E)
concepts.realWorld: Dependency resolution, clustering, network connectivity.

concepts.title: Weighted adjacency list
concepts.overview: Weighted graphs attach costs to edges. Dijkstra chooses the cheapest-known unvisited frontier for nonnegative weights; Bellman-Ford handles negative edges by repeated relaxation; MST algorithms minimize total edge cost required to connect vertices rather than shortest path distances.
concepts.mentalModel: The same graph can answer different questions: shortest journey to a target or cheapest overall connected network. Those objectives are not interchangeable.
concepts.whenToUse: Use shortest path for routing, transit and latency; MST for cabling or infrastructure; Bellman-Ford where negative edges may occur.
concepts.tradeoffs: Dijkstra with adjacency-list heap costs roughly O((V+E)log V); Bellman-Ford O(VE); Kruskal O(E log E).
concepts.commonMistakes: Using Dijkstra on negative-weight edges, overlooking stale heap entries, or substituting an MST for a shortest-path tree.
concepts.operations: Dijkstra O((V+E)log V) heap; Bellman-Ford O(VE); Floyd O(V³)
concepts.realWorld: Routing, delivery planning, cloud network optimization.

concepts.title: DP table
concepts.overview: Dynamic programming avoids solving the same overlapping subproblem repeatedly. Define precisely what the state means, write its recurrence and base cases, then choose recursion+memoization or iterative tabulation. A small state often needs only a few prior values.
concepts.mentalModel: For stair counting, ways(i)=ways(i-1)+ways(i-2). Save each answer once instead of branching exponentially into two recursive calls every time.
concepts.whenToUse: Use when optimal/counting choices have repeated subproblems and optimal substructure, such as house robber, coin change and decoding.
concepts.tradeoffs: Memoization stores reached states; tabulation visits states systematically. Rolling variables reduce memory if only recent states are required.
concepts.commonMistakes: Wrong initialization (especially empty prefix), optimizing memory before proving the recurrence, or assuming a greedy choice is valid.
concepts.operations: Usually O(states × transition cost) time; space O(states) or optimized
concepts.realWorld: Optimization, planning, throttling and sequence decisions.

concepts.title: 2D DP matrix
concepts.overview: Two-dimensional DP tracks two independent progress coordinates, such as how much of each string has been matched or which row/column of a grid is being processed. A recurrence depends on neighboring smaller states and must respect dependency order.
concepts.mentalModel: For LCS(i,j), when final characters match, add one to LCS(i-1,j-1); otherwise take the best of dropping one character from either prefix.
concepts.whenToUse: Use for string matching/editing, knapsack with capacity, grid path counting and subsequence comparisons.
concepts.tradeoffs: Standard table uses O(mn) time and memory; many row-local recurrences compress space to O(n).
concepts.commonMistakes: Using substring instead of subsequence, iterating capacity forward in 0/1 knapsack, or overwriting a DP cell before saving the previous diagonal.
concepts.operations: Often O(nm) time and space; rolling rows reduce memory when valid
concepts.realWorld: Diff engines, DNA similarity, cost optimization.

concepts.title: Bitmask
concepts.overview: Integers are bit vectors. AND tests overlapping one-bits, OR combines flags, XOR toggles and cancels equal bits, and shifts move bit positions. Number-theory routines such as gcd and prime sieves use arithmetic invariants rather than bit tricks.
concepts.mentalModel: XOR acts like a toggle switch: x^x=0 and x^0=x. Therefore duplicates cancel in pairs, leaving the unmatched value.
concepts.whenToUse: Use bitmasks for compact feature flags, subset states, parity problems, arithmetic shortcuts and low-level protocols.
concepts.tradeoffs: Fixed-width Java ints have 32 bits; bitwise loops are O(1) in machine-word terms. Numeric algorithms have their own complexity depending on bounds.
concepts.commonMistakes: Confusing >> with >>>, overflow or sign extension, and forgetting operator precedence in bit expressions.
concepts.operations: Bit checks O(1) per machine word; gcd O(log min(a,b))
concepts.realWorld: Permissions, compression, protocol flags, Bloom-filter internals.

concepts.title: Fenwick / segment tree
concepts.overview: Fenwick trees store partial prefix sums in an indexed array, supporting point update and prefix sum in O(log n). Segment trees recursively represent ranges and combine children, supporting a wider set of operations (min, max, sum, lazy range update).
concepts.mentalModel: Fenwick jumps by the lowest set bit to move between aggregate buckets. A segment tree splits [left,right] recursively and stores an aggregate at each internal node.
concepts.whenToUse: Use for mutable sums, ranking, frequency tables, scheduling interval overlap and dynamic range queries.
concepts.tradeoffs: Fenwick is compact O(n) memory and easy for prefix operations; segment trees have more flexibility but greater code and memory cost.
concepts.commonMistakes: Forgetting Fenwick's one-based indexing, mixing inclusive and exclusive endpoints, or pushing lazy updates incorrectly.
concepts.operations: Build Fenwick O(n log n) naive / O(n) optimized; update/query O(log n)
concepts.realWorld: Live counters, range analytics, leaderboard updates.

concepts.title: HashMap + doubly linked list
concepts.overview: Data-structure design problems combine primitives to meet a public API's performance contract. An LRU cache needs hash lookup plus a recency-ordered doubly linked list (or LinkedHashMap); streaming medians need two heaps; a randomized set needs a hash index and dense array.

concepts.title: Hash lookup
concepts.overview: A hash lookup makes previous values immediately addressable by key. Instead of checking every pair, store each number while scanning and ask whether the required complement has already been seen.

concepts.title: Fixed window
concepts.overview: A fixed-size window tracks an aggregate for a specific number of consecutive elements. When the window slides, remove the outgoing element and add the incoming one rather than recomputing from scratch.

concepts.commonMistakes: Forgetting to remove nums[r-k], resulting in a growing prefix sum rather than a fixed window.

concepts.title: Variable window
concepts.overview: A variable-length window expands until a condition becomes true, then shrinks to find a shorter valid answer. Correctness requires that changing window boundaries behaves monotonically for the chosen condition.

concepts.whenToUse: Shortest positive-sum intervals, longest unique substring and at-most-k constraints.
concepts.tradeoffs: Two pointers give O(n); if monotonicity fails, prefix sums plus a monotonic deque or map may be required.
concepts.commonMistakes: Applying the same proof to negative arrays, where sums can decrease after expansion or increase after shrinking.

concepts.whenToUse: In-place linked-list reversal, palindrome checks and rearrangement.

concepts.title: Monotonic stack
concepts.overview: A monotonic stack keeps candidate bars in increasing height order. When a lower bar arrives, all taller bars have found their next smaller element and can finalize the maximum rectangle width.

concepts.whenToUse: Next-greater/smaller queries, histogram area and stock-span patterns.
concepts.tradeoffs: A nested scan can cost O(n²); a monotonic stack pushes and pops each index once.
concepts.commonMistakes: Using the height of the new bar instead of the popped bar when calculating rectangle area.

concepts.title: Monotonic deque
concepts.overview: A decreasing deque stores indices of window elements that can still become the maximum. When a new value arrives, discard dominated smaller values from the back and remove expired indices from the front.

concepts.title: Heap select top-K

concepts.whenToUse: Top-K frequency, closest points and continuously updated rankings.

concepts.commonMistakes: Using a max-heap holding all n items when a min-heap of size k would save memory.

concepts.overview: DFS recursively explores each reachable neighbor before returning. Mark visited immediately; otherwise cycles and multiple grid routes repeat nodes. Each component requires one outer starting visit.

concepts.title: Advanced DP
concepts.overview: Interval DP handles problems where the best result for range [l,r] depends on splitting around a chosen last action. Choosing the last balloon keeps neighbors outside the interval fixed and makes left/right subproblems independent.
concepts.mentalModel: dp[l][r] is optimal coins from removing only l..r while retaining boundary neighbors.
concepts.whenToUse: Parenthesization, optimal interval scheduling, bursting balloons and matrix-chain DP.
concepts.tradeoffs: O(n³) time, O(n²) memory.
concepts.commonMistakes: Choosing the first popped item yields dependencies on future neighbor changes and breaks the simple recurrence.
concepts.realWorld: Practice and implement the linked example, then adapt the same invariant to new inputs.

concepts.codeLabel: Applied Java example: Burst Balloons
steps: Pad array with 1 on both ends
